planting.note: Plant after last frost on a sturdy overhead trellis in full sun; this dioecious vine needs a compatible male Actinidia chinensis pollinator nearby, and should be sited with excellent airflow to reduce bacterial canker pressure.

directions: Hort16A was the pioneering gold-fleshed kiwifruit selection bred by New Zealand researchers and brought to market by Zespri in the late 1990s as Zespri Gold, the smooth, hairless, beaked bronze-skinned fruit that first introduced sweet, low-acid golden kiwifruit to world markets ahead of green Hayward types. Its tender, aromatic yellow flesh and mild tropical sweetness drove rapid export growth through the early 2000s, but the vine proved highly vulnerable to Pseudomonas syringae pv. actinidiae (Psa) bacterial canker, which devastated plantings first in Italy and then New Zealand from the late 2000s onward, collapsing whole orchards of this cultivar within a few seasons of infection. Because of that vulnerability it has been almost entirely replaced in commercial production by the hardier, Psa-tolerant 'Zesy002' (SunGold), and today it survives mainly in legacy plantings, breeding collections, and the occasional home garden. Where still grown, give it the same overhead trellis, male pollinator, and open, well-ventilated canopy recommended for other golden kiwifruit, and watch closely for canker symptoms such as stem bleeding or wilting shoots.
sources: New Zealand Journal of Crop and Horticultural Science

common_name: Rume Sudan Coffee (South Sudan Boma Plateau Wild Arabica Landrace)

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Rume Sudan is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Rume Sudan is a wild Arabica landrace originating on the Boma Plateau of South Sudan, genetically distinct from the Ethiopian landraces that gave rise to most cultivated Arabica and increasingly recognized as a second center of origin for the species. Early twentieth-century observers noted its unusual freedom from coffee berry disease, and it has since become valued breeding stock for that trait, even though the plant itself is not notably resistant to coffee leaf rust. Growers and cuppers who have evaluated it describe an exceptional, wine-like cup quality uncommon in disease-resistant breeding material, which has made it a sought-after parent in programs aiming to combine wild-genetic disease tolerance with good flavor rather than relying solely on robusta-derived rust resistance. The shrub itself is unremarkable in form, resembling other tall heirloom Typica-type Arabica, so give it the same rich, humus-heavy, well-drained acidic soil, filtered shade, and multi-year wait before first harvest expected of other wild and landrace Arabica selections.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

common_name: New Mexico No. 6 Chile (Early NMSU Low-Heat Green Chile, Parent of New Mexico 6-4)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; New Mexico No. 6 is an early New Mexico State University green chile release grown the same way as later Hatch-type selections.

directions: New Mexico No. 6 was released in 1950 by Dr. Roy Harper at New Mexico State University in Las Cruces, selected in 1947 from an unnamed local chile population growing in the Mesilla Valley. Compared with Fabian Garcia's earlier New Mexico No. 9, its pods dried roughly a fifth faster and carried only about half the pungency, qualities that suited it well to the chile processing industry as well as the fresh green chile market. It served directly as the parent stock for New Mexico No. 6-4, selected from it in 1957 to reduce pod heat even further, and that later selection went on to become the long-running commercial standard for New Mexico green chile while New Mexico No. 6 itself faded from wide cultivation. Grow it exactly as later NMSU green chile releases: start indoors, transplant after frost danger passes into full sun and well-drained soil, and harvest pods green for roasting or allow them to ripen fully red for drying and grinding.
sources: New Mexico State University — The Chile Cultivars of New Mexico State University, 1913-2022
Paul W. Bosland and David Votava, 'Peppers: Vegetable and Spice Capsicums' (CABI, 2012)
